alt="IMG_2231.jpg" is a camera filename. It passes any rule that only checks an alt attribute is present and non-empty, and conveys nothing: a listener learns that a file exists, not that this is a photograph of the author being featured.
The same portrait, named "Ursula Vane, photographed at the 2019 festival" — it identifies the person and the occasion, which is what the image is on the page to convey.

alt="chart" names the format and withholds the content. The chart is the only place the monthly borrowing figures appear, so a listener gets none of the data the page exists to present. Naming the genre of an image is not an alternative to it.

The same chart, with the trend and its figures in the alt ("a rise from January to a May peak of 1,240, then a decline to 780 in August") and a link to the full table beneath it. The information in the image is available without the image.

alt="decorative divider line" describes the image instead of removing it. The rule is that a decorative image takes alt="" so assistive technology skips it; giving it text makes a screen reader announce a horizontal rule as content. The word "decorative" in an accessible name is itself the evidence the author knew it carried no meaning.
The same divider with alt="" and role="presentation" — correctly removed from the accessibility tree, so it is never announced.

An informative chart marked decorative with alt="". This is the inverse of the usual error and the reason a rule engine cannot settle 1.1.1: axe is satisfied, because an empty alt is valid markup. The surrounding prose makes claims about loans rising and falling for which this chart is the only evidence, so hiding it removes information rather than noise. Deciding this needs somebody to look at the image and read the text around it.

A genuinely decorative rule with alt="" and role="presentation". The twin of the lending-summary case: identical markup, opposite correct answer, because this image carries nothing the page depends on. The pair is here so a checker cannot score by preferring one answer for empty alt.

The cover's alt repeats the figcaption immediately below it, so the title is announced twice in succession. Redundant text is a real harm — it doubles the length of the list without adding anything — but the alternative reading is that a named cover is better than an unnamed one, and an author could defend either. A confident verdict in either direction over-claims; the correct behaviour is to route this to a person. Scored as over-confidence if a checker answers pass or fail here.

rationale: alt="library" on a photograph inside a "Visit us" panel. Whether this image is informative (showing what the reading room looks like before you travel) or decorative (a mood photograph beside the address) depends on authorial intent, which is not recoverable from the page. One vague word is a poor alternative either way, but the right answer is that a person should decide.

rationale: The photograph of the local history room is named "photo". That names the format and withholds everything else: a listener learns an image is present and nothing about what is in it. The picture shows wide oak map cabinets along two walls, a framed county map above them and a globe on a wooden stand, and none of that appears anywhere else — the surrounding text gives the floor and the staffed hours only. All five photographs on this page follow the same pattern, so the page is a list of five rooms that cannot be told apart by ear. An alt attribute is present and non-empty, so nothing that only checks for presence has anything to report.
